versions.question: A web request enters a classic three-tier design on AWS. Which sequence shows the tiers it passes through, from first to last?
options: DNS resolution, then a public load balancer, then private application servers, then the database tier
Private application servers, then a public load balancer, then DNS resolution, then the database tier
Database tier, then application servers, then a public load balancer, then DNS resolution
A public load balancer, then DNS resolution, then the database tier, then private application servers
versions.explanation: Traffic gets more private at each hop: Route 53, public ALB, private EC2 Auto Scaling group, then data subnets.
option_explanations: Correct. Traffic gets more private at each hop, starting with DNS.
Wrong order: the app servers sit behind the load balancer, not in front of it.
This is reversed; the database is the last tier, never the first.
DNS resolves first, and the database is reached only via the app tier.

versions.question: In a standard AWS web architecture, which tier talks directly to the RDS and ElastiCache layer?
options: The Application Load Balancer, which queries the database for its targets
The EC2 instances of the Auto Scaling group in the private subnets
Route 53, which reads from the cache to answer DNS queries here
The end user's browser, through a public database endpoint, directly
versions.explanation: The ALB only forwards to the app tier; the app tier in private subnets reads and writes the data tier.
option_explanations: Wrong: an ALB forwards to targets and never queries the database.
Correct. The app tier in private subnets reads and writes the data tier.
Route 53 answers DNS queries; it doesn't read from a cache.
Browsers don't connect to a database directly; it sits in private subnets.

versions.question: After saving a change, an app's next query on an RDS read replica still returns the previous value for a moment. What explains this?
options: Replicas only refresh once a day during the backup window
The replica is a synchronous Multi-AZ standby and rejects reads until failover
Replication from the primary is asynchronous, so the replica may be slightly behind
Writes are queued by the primary until every replica acknowledges them
versions.explanation: Read replicas use asynchronous replication, so lag is normal. Use the primary when you need read-after-write consistency.
option_explanations: Replicas are updated continuously, not once a day.
A Multi-AZ standby isn't readable and isn't a read replica.
Correct. Replicas are asynchronous, so they can lag slightly.
The primary doesn't wait for replicas; that would be synchronous replication.

versions.question: An application needs read-after-write consistency for user settings on an RDS database with read replicas. Where should it read those settings from?
options: Any replica, because replication is synchronous and always current
The replica in the same AZ, since it receives writes first
A Multi-AZ standby, which serves reads with zero lag
The primary DB instance, which holds every committed write
versions.explanation: Replicas are asynchronous and can lag; the primary always has the latest committed write. A Multi-AZ standby is not readable.
option_explanations: Replicas are asynchronous, so they can return stale data.
A same-AZ replica gets writes asynchronously, like any replica.
A Multi-AZ standby can't serve reads at all.
Correct. The primary always has the latest committed write.

versions.question: VPC Flow Logs can be created at which scopes? (Choose three)
options: A single network interface
A Network ACL rule
A Route 53 record set
A whole VPC
A single subnet
versions.explanation: Flow logs attach to a VPC, subnet or ENI; narrower scopes limit the volume of records.
option_explanations: Correct: flow logs can be attached to a single ENI.
Flow logs attach to VPCs, subnets or ENIs, not to NACL rules.
Route 53 records are DNS entries, not a flow log scope.
Correct: a flow log can cover the whole VPC.
Correct: a flow log can cover a single subnet.

versions.question: To capture IP traffic metadata for just one EC2 instance's network card, which resources could you attach a flow log to? (Choose two)
options: The instance's IAM role
The subnet containing the instance
The AMI used to launch it
The security group on the instance
The instance's elastic network interface
versions.explanation: A flow log may be created on an ENI, its subnet or the whole VPC, never on IAM roles, AMIs or security groups.
option_explanations: An IAM role isn't a network resource, so no flow log can attach.
Correct: a subnet flow log includes the instance's ENI, though also its neighbors.
An AMI is an image template, not a flow log scope.
Security groups aren't flow log targets; they filter traffic.
Correct: the ENI is the narrowest scope for one instance's card.

versions.question: Which items can software on an EC2 instance read from the instance metadata endpoint? (Choose three)
options: Its availability zone
The name of its instance profile role
The full JSON policy documents of that role
The account's root access keys
Short-lived credentials for its instance role
versions.explanation: IMDS exposes the role name and temporary credentials, but not the role's policy documents.
option_explanations: Correct: availability zone is available under meta-data/placement.
Correct: IMDS shows the instance profile's role name.
IMDS doesn't return policy documents; those come from IAM.
Root access keys are never exposed through instance metadata.
Correct: IMDS serves temporary credentials for the attached role.

versions.question: Which are true about querying 169.254.169.254 from an instance? (Choose two)
options: It lists every other instance in the VPC
It returns the account password
It can return the instance ID and hostname
It returns the Allow and Deny statements of the role's policies
It returns the role name and its rotating credentials
versions.explanation: Metadata includes instance details and role credentials. Policy contents must be fetched through IAM instead.
option_explanations: IMDS only describes the instance itself, not other instances.
Account passwords are never exposed through metadata.
Correct: instance ID and hostname are in the metadata.
Policy statements aren't exposed; use IAM APIs for those.
Correct: it returns the role name and rotating temporary credentials.

versions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts an RDS Multi-AZ standby with a read replica?
options: The standby copies data synchronously and cannot serve queries; a replica copies asynchronously and can serve SELECTs
The standby copies data asynchronously and serves reads; a replica copies synchronously and cannot serve queries
Both copy synchronously, but only the standby has its own endpoint for reads
Both are readable, but the replica fails over automatically while the standby must be promoted by hand
versions.explanation: Multi-AZ is for HA with synchronous replication and automatic failover; replicas scale reads with asynchronous replication.
option_explanations: Correct: the standby is synchronous and unreadable; the replica is asynchronous and readable.
This is reversed; the standby is synchronous and can't serve reads.
Replicas are asynchronous, and the standby has no read endpoint.
The standby fails over automatically; replicas must be promoted manually.

versions.question: A team's primary database is overloaded by reporting SELECT queries, and a separate worry is surviving an AZ outage. Which pairing solves both?
options: Multi-AZ for the reporting load and read replicas for the outage protection
Read replicas for the reporting load and Multi-AZ for the outage protection
Only Multi-AZ, because its standby handles the reporting queries too
Only read replicas, because they fail over automatically within the cluster endpoint
versions.explanation: Replicas offload reads but are asynchronous; the Multi-AZ standby is not readable but gives synchronous automatic failover.
option_explanations: Multi-AZ doesn't offload reads, and replicas don't provide HA failover.
Correct: replicas take the reads, Multi-AZ gives AZ failover.
The Multi-AZ standby can't serve queries.
Replicas don't fail over automatically; they need manual promotion.

versions.question: A script on an EC2 instance with no role attached must learn which AZ it runs in. Where can it get that?
options: A call to the Resource Groups Tagging API filtered on the hostname
The CloudWatch agent's local configuration file on its disk
A call to the link-local metadata address on the host
An SQS message published by the hypervisor at boot time
versions.explanation: Instance metadata is served locally by IMDS at 169.254.169.254, including AZ, IDs and IPs, and needs no IAM permissions.
option_explanations: The Tagging API doesn't report an instance's AZ and needs IAM permissions.
The CloudWatch agent config doesn't contain the AZ.
Correct. IMDS at 169.254.169.254 gives the AZ with no IAM permissions.
The hypervisor doesn't publish to SQS.

versions.question: What is true of the endpoint an instance uses to read its own instance ID?
options: It is a public internet endpoint that requires SigV4 signed requests
It is a VPC endpoint that must be created per subnet and secured by a bucket policy
It is a regional service API that requires ec2:DescribeInstances
It is link-local, reachable only from the instance, with no IAM permissions needed
versions.explanation: IMDS is local to the host and unauthenticated by IAM, which is why IMDSv2 adds session tokens.
option_explanations: IMDS isn't public and doesn't use SigV4 signing.
IMDS isn't a VPC endpoint, and bucket policies don't apply.
It isn't a regional API, and ec2:DescribeInstances isn't needed.
Correct. IMDS is link-local, instance-only, and needs no IAM permissions.

versions.question: Versioning is on. Someone issues a plain DELETE for `report.pdf` with no version ID. What does the bucket now show?
options: A delete marker is added and older versions remain
Only the immediately previous version is removed and the rest stay
The request is refused with an error unless MFA is used for it
Every version is erased at once and storage billing stops now
versions.explanation: A delete without a version ID adds a delete marker. Removing the marker restores the object.
option_explanations: Correct. A plain DELETE adds a delete marker; older versions stay.
A plain DELETE removes no version; it only adds a marker.
A plain DELETE isn't refused; MFA applies only if MFA Delete is configured.
Nothing is erased, so storage billing continues.

versions.question: How can you permanently remove one particular version of an object in a versioned bucket?
options: Issue a plain DELETE on the key
Issue a DELETE that names its version ID
Add a lifecycle rule that creates delete markers
Suspend versioning, then re-upload the file
versions.explanation: Only a delete that specifies the version ID is permanent; a plain delete merely hides the object behind a marker.
option_explanations: A plain DELETE only adds a delete marker; the version stays.
Correct. Only a DELETE naming the version ID is permanent.
Lifecycle delete markers don't permanently remove a specific version.
Suspending versioning doesn't remove existing versions.

versions.question: With IMDSv2, how does an instance obtain the session token before reading metadata?
options: Send a GET to `/latest/meta-data/token` with its access key
Call sts:GetSessionToken and place the result in the URL
Send an HTTP PUT to `/latest/api/token` with a TTL header
Send a POST to `/latest/user-data` and parse the response
versions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires a PUT with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds`, then each GET includes the token header.
option_explanations: The token endpoint is /latest/api/token and uses PUT, not GET.
sts:GetSessionToken is unrelated to the IMDSv2 token.
Correct. IMDSv2 uses a PUT with a TTL header to get a token.
/latest/user-data holds launch scripts and isn't a token endpoint.

versions.question: In IMDSv2, which header carries the token on a metadata GET request?
options: Authorization: Bearer with a SigV4 signature
X-Amz-Security-Token
X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds
X-aws-ec2-metadata-token
versions.explanation: After the PUT returns a token, each GET passes it in `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token`. The TTL header is only used on the PUT.
option_explanations: IMDS doesn't use SigV4 or Bearer authorization.
That's the STS credential header, not the IMDS token.
That TTL header is only sent on the PUT that requests the token.
Correct. Each GET passes the token in this header.

versions.question: An online shop wants customers in Japan to see Japanese pricing pages, customers in Brazil Portuguese ones, and everyone else the global site. Which Route 53 routing policy matches?
options: Geolocation routing, with a default record as the catch-all
Latency routing, so each user hits the fastest Region
Weighted routing, with a 50/50 split between both sites
Failover routing, with the global site as primary and a regional site as backup
versions.explanation: Geolocation routes by user location (most specific match), and a Default record covers everything else.
option_explanations: Correct. Geolocation routes by user location; Default catches the rest.
Latency routing picks the lowest-latency Region, not language or country.
Weighted routing splits traffic by proportion, ignoring location.
Failover is for primary/backup availability, not location.

versions.question: A Route 53 geolocation setup has records for France and Germany only. What happens to a user in Canada?
options: They get the Region with the best latency automatically
They are served the Default record, if one has been created
They receive the France record, as the nearest match
Route 53 returns the Germany record at random each time
versions.explanation: Geolocation doesn't fall back to nearest; unmatched users need a Default record.
option_explanations: Geolocation doesn't use latency; unmatched users need a Default record.
Correct. Unmatched users get the Default record, if it exists.
Geolocation has no nearest-match fallback.
There is no random selection; an unmatched user gets no answer without a Default.

versions.question: A regulator requires a firm's data to stay in one country. What should drive the choice of AWS Region before anything else?
options: The Region with the most Availability Zones available
The Region where each service is cheapest this quarter
Whether the Region's location satisfies the legal data-residency rule
The Region closest to the engineers who deploy the code
versions.explanation: Compliance is a hard constraint: Regions that don't satisfy it are discarded before comparing latency, services or price.
option_explanations: More AZs help availability but don't decide legal compliance.
Price is a later trade-off, not a hard constraint.
Correct. Compliance is a hard constraint that eliminates Regions first.
Engineer location doesn't matter for where data must reside.

versions.question: Which factor eliminates candidate Regions outright, rather than merely ranking them?
options: A small price difference per GB of storage
Latency of a few milliseconds to a subset of users
A newly launched service that is not yet in the Region
A legal requirement on where data must stay
versions.explanation: Compliance is binary; latency, price and service availability are trade-offs to optimize afterwards.
option_explanations: A small price gap only ranks Regions; it doesn't exclude any.
A few ms of latency is a trade-off, not an elimination criterion.
A missing service is a ranking factor, since you can often use another Region.
Correct. A legal data-location rule rules Regions out outright.

versions.question: A pipeline only needs the metadata header stored in the first 100 bytes of huge S3 objects. How should it read them?
options: Issue GET requests with a Range header for bytes 0-99
Enable Transfer Acceleration and download each file fully
Use S3 Select's multipart upload mode
Copy each object to another bucket then read it
versions.explanation: Byte-range fetches return only the requested part, saving time and data transfer.
option_explanations: Correct. A Range GET fetches only bytes 0-99.
Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers but still downloads whole objects.
S3 Select queries content, and has no multipart upload mode.
Copying first adds cost and time and doesn't help read a header.

versions.question: What is one use of S3 byte-range fetches besides speeding up a large download?
options: Encrypting part of an object with a separate key from KMS
Retrieving only part of an object, such as a header
Moving part of an object to Glacier after thirty days
Versioning only part of a large file in the bucket
versions.explanation: Range GETs can parallelize big downloads, and also fetch just a slice of an object.
option_explanations: Encryption keys apply to whole objects, not byte ranges.
Correct. A Range GET retrieves just a slice such as a header.
Lifecycle transitions move whole objects, not parts.
Versioning applies to whole objects, not parts.

versions.question: A bucket has MFA Delete on. Which operations need an MFA code? (Choose two)
options: Changing versioning to suspended
Deleting a specific object version for good
Reading a previous version of an object
Uploading a new object version
Adding a tag to an object
versions.explanation: MFA Delete only guards destructive operations: permanent version deletion and suspending versioning.
option_explanations: Correct. Suspending versioning requires MFA when MFA Delete is on.
Correct. Permanently deleting a version needs an MFA code.
Reads aren't destructive, so no MFA is needed.
Uploads aren't guarded by MFA Delete.
Tagging isn't a destructive action requiring MFA.

versions.question: Which two requests are protected when MFA Delete is configured? (Choose two)
options: Listing the bucket contents
PUT of new objects
Turning versioning off on the bucket
Permanent removal of a version ID
Creating a delete marker with a plain DELETE
versions.explanation: A plain delete just adds a marker, so it doesn't need MFA; permanent deletes and suspending versioning do.
option_explanations: Listing is a read and needs no MFA.
Uploads don't require MFA.
Correct. Changing versioning state requires MFA.
Correct. Permanently deleting a version ID requires MFA.
A plain DELETE only adds a marker and needs no MFA.

versions.question: A video company wants to slowly increase the share of users sent to its eu-west-1 stack and decrease eu-central-1, using geographic closeness. Which Route 53 option fits?
options: Weighted routing with equal weights on both of the records
Multivalue answer routing with health checks on each target
Geoproximity routing, raising the bias for eu-west-1 in Traffic Flow
Failover routing with eu-west-1 as secondary and eu-central-1 as primary
versions.explanation: Geoproximity shifts traffic by distance, with bias values that expand or shrink a Region's reach.
option_explanations: Equal weights split traffic evenly by proportion, not by distance.
Multivalue returns several healthy records; it doesn't shift by geography.
Correct. Bias grows or shrinks a resource's geographic reach.
Failover sends traffic to the secondary only when the primary is unhealthy.

versions.question: What does a negative bias do in Route 53 geoproximity routing?
options: It blocks all queries from reaching that resource
It raises the record's TTL to its maximum
It makes the resource act as a failover secondary
It shrinks the geographic area whose traffic goes to that resource
versions.explanation: Positive bias (1 to 99) expands a resource's area; negative bias (-1 to -99) shrinks it.
option_explanations: Bias doesn't block traffic; it adjusts the area served.
Bias has no effect on TTL.
Bias doesn't create failover behavior.
Correct. Negative bias shrinks the area routed to that resource.

versions.question: A research group must train neural networks and needs instances with attached GPUs. Which EC2 category covers this?
options: Accelerated computing, such as the P and G families
Compute optimized, for high-frequency batch CPU work
Storage optimized, with NVMe local disks
Memory optimized, for large in-memory databases
versions.explanation: Accelerated computing instances use GPUs or other hardware accelerators for ML and graphics.
option_explanations: Correct. P and G families have GPUs for ML training.
Compute optimized targets CPU-bound work, not GPUs.
Storage optimized targets high local disk throughput and IOPS.
Memory optimized targets large in-memory workloads, not GPUs.

versions.question: A team picks a G or P family EC2 instance. What type of category are they selecting?
options: General purpose
Accelerated computing
Storage optimized
Memory optimized, with high RAM per vCPU
versions.explanation: G and P families carry GPUs and belong to accelerated computing.
option_explanations: General purpose has no GPUs; it balances CPU and memory.
Correct. G and P families have GPUs and are accelerated computing.
Storage optimized targets high local IOPS, not GPUs.
Memory optimized targets high RAM per vCPU, not GPUs.

versions.question: When you register and host a domain in Route 53, which charges apply? (Choose two)
options: A charge for creating Alias records to CloudFront
A monthly charge for each hosted zone
A fee for each health check that is deleted
An annual domain registration charge
A one-time setup fee per DNS record
versions.explanation: Route 53 charges for hosted zones and domain registration, plus queries (Alias queries to AWS resources are free).
option_explanations: Alias queries and records to AWS resources are free.
Correct. Each hosted zone has a monthly charge.
Health checks are billed monthly, not per deletion.
Correct. Registering a domain carries an annual fee.
There is no per-record setup fee.

versions.question: Which are real costs of running a domain on Route 53? (Choose two)
options: A charge for every Alias query to an ELB
Yearly renewal of the registered domain
A charge per Region the zone is replicated in
A fee charged for each new record created
Monthly cost of each hosted zone
versions.explanation: Zones and registration are billed; Alias queries to AWS resources are not.
option_explanations: Alias queries to AWS resources like ELB are free.
Correct. A registered domain is renewed yearly at a charge.
Hosted zones aren't billed per Region of replication.
Creating records is free.
Correct. Each hosted zone is billed monthly.

versions.question: In a cache-aside pattern with Redis, which line after loading the user from the database stores it so it disappears after 10 minutes?
options: `r.set(key, json.dumps(user), nx=600)`
`r.persist(key, json.dumps(user))`
`r.set(key, json.dumps(user), ex=600)`
`r.rename(key, 600)`
versions.explanation: `ex` sets a time-to-live in seconds, limiting how stale lazy-loaded data can get.
option_explanations: nx isn't a TTL option; it only sets the key if absent.
persist removes a TTL; it doesn't set one and takes no value.
Correct. ex sets expiry in seconds, so it lasts 10 minutes.
rename changes a key name and has nothing to do with TTL.

versions.question: Why add a TTL when writing to the cache in a lazy-loading strategy?
options: To make the cache write synchronous with every database commit
To encrypt cached items in memory at rest on the node
To let the database replicate the item to its read replicas
To limit how long stale data can persist
versions.explanation: Lazy loading can serve stale values; expiry caps the staleness.
option_explanations: A TTL doesn't affect write synchronization.
TTL is about expiry, not encryption.
TTL doesn't involve database replication.
Correct. Expiry caps how long stale data can persist.

versions.question: An IAM policy statement has Sid, Action and Resource only. Which required element is absent, making it fail?
options: Effect, which states Allow or Deny
Principal, which an identity-based policy always requires
Condition, which is needed for any S3 action to work
Version, which must be repeated inside each statement
versions.explanation: Every statement needs `Effect`. `Principal` is only for resource-based and trust policies; Condition and Sid are optional.
option_explanations: Correct. Effect (Allow or Deny) is mandatory in every statement.
Principal isn't used in identity-based policies.
Condition is optional.
Version is a top-level policy element, not per statement.

versions.question: Which element of an IAM policy statement decides whether the listed actions are permitted or refused?
options: Sid
Effect
Condition
Resource
versions.explanation: `Effect` is Allow or Deny and is mandatory in every statement.
option_explanations: Sid is an optional identifier.
Correct. Effect is Allow or Deny and decides the outcome.
Condition adds optional restrictions; it doesn't decide the outcome.
Resource says which objects the statement applies to, not Allow or Deny.

versions.question: Using the AWS CLI or an SDK, how long at most can an S3 pre-signed URL stay valid?
options: Up to 24 hours (1 day)
Up to 72 hours (3 days)
Up to 168 hours (7 days)
Up to 720 hours (30 days)
versions.explanation: CLI/SDK allow up to 168 hours (7 days); the console limits you to 12 hours.
option_explanations: That's too short; the CLI/SDK limit is 7 days.
3 days is below the CLI/SDK maximum.
Correct. CLI and SDK allow up to 168 hours.
30 days exceeds the 7-day maximum.

versions.question: Which expiry limit is correct for pre-signed URLs generated in the S3 console?
options: 7 days
1 hour
30 minutes
12 hours
versions.explanation: Console: up to 12 hours. CLI/SDK: up to 168 hours.
option_explanations: 7 days is the CLI/SDK limit; the console allows less.
The console allows more than 1 hour.
The console allows more than 30 minutes.
Correct. The console caps pre-signed URLs at 12 hours.

versions.question: Instances in a subnet cannot connect out, and the team wants records showing each connection's ACCEPT or REJECT outcome. Which feature provides them?
options: VPC Flow Logs on the subnet or ENI
AWS Config rules on the route table of the subnet
CloudTrail data events for the instances involved
AWS Trusted Advisor security checks on the account
versions.explanation: Flow logs record accepted and rejected traffic at the VPC, subnet or ENI level.
option_explanations: Correct. Flow logs record ACCEPT or REJECT per connection.
Config tracks resource configuration, not per-connection outcomes.
CloudTrail data events log API activity on resources, not network traffic.
Trusted Advisor gives account checks, not connection records.

versions.question: Which tool shows whether a security group or network ACL rejected specific packets to an ENI?
options: CloudTrail network activity events
Flow logs on the ENI or subnet
AWS Config network rules history
CloudWatch agent memory metrics
versions.explanation: CloudTrail records API calls, not packets. Flow logs include an action field of ACCEPT or REJECT.
option_explanations: CloudTrail records API calls, not packet accept/reject.
Correct. Flow logs include an ACCEPT or REJECT action field.
Config records configuration history, not packet decisions.
CloudWatch agent memory metrics have nothing to do with network rejects.

versions.question: Which subnet placement follows best practice for a three-tier web app with a load balancer, application servers and a database?
options: Load balancer and application servers private, database public
All three tiers public, with restrictive security groups
Load balancer public; application servers and database in private subnets
Application servers public, load balancer and database private
versions.explanation: Only the ALB needs to face the internet; app and data tiers stay private.
option_explanations: The database shouldn't be public, and the ALB needs to be.
Public app and database tiers expand the attack surface.
Correct. Only the ALB faces the internet; the rest stays private.
The ALB must be public to receive internet traffic.

versions.question: In a three-tier AWS layout, why are the RDS instances placed in data subnets without a route to the internet gateway?
options: RDS cannot be launched into public subnets at all
The load balancer must reach the database directly for health checks
Private subnets are required for Multi-AZ to function
Only the app tier should reach them
versions.explanation: Least exposure: the DB accepts traffic only from the app tier, never the internet.
option_explanations: RDS can be launched in public subnets; it just shouldn't be.
Load balancers talk to the app tier, not to the database.
Multi-AZ works regardless of subnet type.
Correct. Only the app tier needs to reach the database.

versions.question: An instance in a private subnet downloads patches from the internet. Which sequence describes the path of the packets?
options: Instance, then the private route table, then a NAT gateway in a public subnet, then the internet gateway
Instance, then the internet gateway, then a NAT gateway in a private subnet
Instance, then a NAT gateway in the same private subnet, then a VPC peering connection
Instance, then the public route table, then the private route table, then the NAT gateway
versions.explanation: The private route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway, which sits in a public subnet whose route table points at the IGW.
option_explanations: Correct. The NAT gateway sits in a public subnet routed to the IGW.
The NAT gateway must be in a public subnet, and it sits before the IGW.
VPC peering isn't used for internet access.
Instances use only their own private route table.

versions.question: Where must a NAT gateway be placed so that private-subnet instances can reach the internet through it?
options: In the same private subnet as the instances using it
In a public subnet routed to the IGW
In a subnet whose route table has no entries at all
Attached to the private subnet's network ACL as a rule
versions.explanation: The NAT gateway itself needs internet access via an IGW, so it lives in a public subnet.
option_explanations: A NAT in a private subnet has no route to the internet.
Correct. The NAT needs an IGW route, so it lives in a public subnet.
The NAT gateway needs routes to the IGW.
NACLs filter traffic and don't host NAT gateways.

versions.question: The Route 53 health check on a public ALB endpoint fails continuously, yet browsing to the site works. What is the most likely cause?
options: The hosted zone has too many records for health checks to run properly
The ALB's DNS name is longer than health checks are able to support
The ALB security group blocks the Route 53 health checkers
The ALB listener uses a TTL above 60 seconds on its records
versions.explanation: Health checkers come from published IP ranges that must be allowed by the security group or firewall.
option_explanations: Record count doesn't stop health checks.
DNS name length isn't a limit for health checks.
Correct. The security group must allow Route 53 health checker IPs.
Record TTL doesn't affect health checks.

versions.question: To make a Route 53 health check succeed for an endpoint behind a restrictive security group, what should you do?
options: Add the hosted zone ID to the security group's outbound rules
Associate an Elastic IP with the health check
Raise the record's weight so more probes get through
Allow inbound traffic from the Route 53 health checker IP ranges
versions.explanation: Health checks originate from AWS-published IPs and need inbound access to the endpoint.
option_explanations: Outbound rules and a zone ID don't let checkers in.
Health checks don't use Elastic IPs.
Weight has no effect on whether probes succeed.
Correct. Allow inbound traffic from the Route 53 checker IP ranges.

versions.question: What does Aurora Backtrack do for a database with a bad UPDATE?
options: Rewinds the cluster in place to an earlier time
Copies snapshots to another Region on a schedule
Adds read replicas that serve the same data
Fails the writer over to a standby in another AZ
versions.explanation: Backtrack rewinds the existing cluster to an earlier time without restoring from a backup.
option_explanations: Correct. Backtrack rewinds the cluster in place.
That describes cross-Region snapshot copying, not Backtrack.
That describes read replicas, not Backtrack.
That describes Multi-AZ failover, not Backtrack.

versions.question: How does Aurora Backtrack differ from point-in-time restore?
options: It copies data to a new Region before restoring it there
It rewinds the cluster itself, with no new cluster
It only works on read replicas and not on the writer
It replays the binary log into a separate standby
versions.explanation: PITR creates a new cluster; Backtrack rewinds in place and can move back and forth.
option_explanations: Backtrack doesn't copy to other Regions.
Correct. Backtrack rewinds in place; PITR creates a new cluster.
Backtrack works on the cluster's writer, not on replicas only.
Backtrack doesn't replay binary logs or use a standby.

versions.question: Which statements about EBS and EFS are accurate? (Choose two)
options: An EBS volume lives in a single AZ, while an EFS file system can be accessed from several AZs
EFS typically costs more per GB than EBS general purpose SSD
EFS is designed mainly for Windows servers
An EBS gp3 volume is regionally replicated and mounted from any AZ
versions.explanation: EBS is AZ-bound and cheaper; EFS is a multi-AZ shared Linux file system billed per use.
option_explanations: Correct. EBS is single-AZ; EFS spans multiple AZs.
Correct. EFS costs more per GB than gp EBS.
EFS is for Linux (NFS), not mainly Windows.
EBS volumes are single-AZ, not regionally replicated.

versions.question: Which are true when comparing EFS to EBS? (Choose two)
options: EFS volumes must be provisioned in advance in GB
EBS volumes are billed only for the data stored, not provisioned size
EFS is for Linux clients and is priced higher than EBS
Many instances in different AZs can mount the same EFS file system
versions.explanation: EFS is shared, multi-AZ, Linux-only, pay-per-use; EBS is provisioned and per-AZ.
option_explanations: EFS grows automatically; you don't provision its size.
EBS is billed for provisioned size, not data stored.
Correct. EFS is Linux-only and costs more than EBS.
Correct. Many instances across AZs can mount one EFS.

versions.question: Each VPC subnet maps to what?
options: Every AZ in the Region at once
A single Region only, with AZ chosen at launch
Exactly one Availability Zone
One account across multiple VPCs
versions.explanation: Subnets are AZ-scoped; use multiple subnets in different AZs for high availability.
option_explanations: A subnet doesn't span multiple AZs.
A subnet is tied to an AZ, not just a Region.
Correct. Each subnet lives in exactly one AZ.
Subnets belong to one VPC, not across VPCs.

versions.question: A team wants an Auto Scaling group to survive the loss of one AZ. What must they do about subnets?
options: Create one large subnet that spans all AZs
Use one subnet and enable cross-zone routing
Place instances in a subnet in another Region
Spread the group across subnets located in different AZs

Subnets are AZ-bound; no cross-zone routing option fixes that.
A subnet in another Region wouldn't be in the same VPC.
Correct. Use subnets in several AZs for resilience.

versions.question: An events company needs to guarantee that 40 instances can launch in us-west-2b for 10 days only, paying On-Demand rates, with no long-term contract. Which purchase option?
options: An On-Demand Capacity Reservation in that AZ
A 3-year Standard Reserved Instance purchase in the Region, paid upfront
A Spot Fleet request with a capacity-optimized allocation strategy
A Savings Plan commitment that covers the whole Region
versions.explanation: Capacity Reservations hold capacity in an AZ for any period; Regional RIs/Savings Plans don't guarantee capacity in an AZ.
option_explanations: Correct. A Capacity Reservation guarantees AZ capacity for any period.
A 3-year RI is a long commitment and regional RIs don't guarantee AZ capacity.
Spot capacity isn't guaranteed and can be interrupted.
Savings Plans give a discount but don't reserve capacity.

versions.question: Which feature reserves EC2 capacity in an AZ with no term commitment, billed at On-Demand rates whether used or not?
options: Spot blocks
Capacity Reservations
Convertible Reserved Instances
Dedicated Hosts
versions.explanation: Capacity Reservations: any duration, specific AZ, charged even when idle.

versions.question: Which data would be risky to serve from a cache, because even slightly stale values cause harm?
options: Product images that are replaced only once a month
Rendered blog articles read by thousands of visitors
Current stock levels or account balances that change constantly
Rarely edited user profile pages and settings
versions.explanation: Cache data that is read often, changes rarely and tolerates staleness.
option_explanations: Images changing monthly are fine to cache.
Articles read often rarely change, which suits caching.
Correct. Fast-changing values like balances can't tolerate staleness.
Rarely edited pages are good cache candidates.

versions.question: When choosing items to cache, which characteristic makes data a good candidate?
options: Updated every few seconds and must be exactly current when read
Written once and never read again by any client
Unique per request, so nothing is ever looked up twice
Read often, changed rarely, tolerant of slightly old values
versions.explanation: Caching pays off with high read-to-write ratios and stale-tolerant data.
option_explanations: Constantly changing exact data is a poor cache fit.
Data never read again gains nothing from caching.
Unique-per-request data never gets a cache hit.
Correct. Read-heavy, rarely changed, stale-tolerant data caches well.

versions.question: Route 53 won't accept a CNAME for `shop.com` itself (no subdomain) pointing at an ELB. What's the fix?

Use a TXT record that contains the ELB's DNS name instead
Create a CNAME for the apex and lower its TTL a lot
Delegate the apex to the ELB with an extra NS record

A TXT record doesn't resolve to the ELB.
A CNAME can't exist at the apex regardless of TTL.
You can't delegate an apex to an ELB via NS records.

versions.question: Why are Alias records preferable to CNAMEs for pointing the root domain at CloudFront?
options: They support any third-party DNS target outside of AWS
They are allowed at the zone apex
They cost more but they offer much longer TTL values
They require the user to maintain the IP list by hand
versions.explanation: CNAMEs can't exist at the apex; Alias records can, for AWS resources.
option_explanations: Alias targets are AWS resources, not any third-party target.
Correct. CNAMEs can't be used at the apex; Alias records can.
Alias records are free to AWS targets, and TTL isn't their selling point.
Alias records follow AWS target IP changes automatically.

versions.question: Which EBS feature keeps deleted snapshots for a configurable period so they can be restored?

EBS Multi-Attach enabled on the volume
Recycle Bin with a retention rule
Elastic Volumes resizing on a live volume

Multi-Attach lets several instances share a volume.
Correct. Recycle Bin retains deleted snapshots per retention rule.
Elastic Volumes resizes live volumes; it doesn't restore deleted snapshots.

versions.question: A retention rule in the Recycle Bin can protect which resources from accidental deletion?
options: Running EC2 instances and their security groups
S3 buckets and the objects stored inside them
Elastic IPs and network interfaces in the VPC
Snapshots and AMIs, via a retention rule
versions.explanation: Recycle Bin supports snapshots and AMIs with retention from 1 day to 1 year.
option_explanations: Recycle Bin doesn't cover instances or security groups.
S3 is not covered; use versioning instead.
Recycle Bin doesn't protect Elastic IPs or ENIs.
Correct. Recycle Bin covers EBS snapshots and AMIs.

versions.question: Which S3 bucket policy statement denies requests that don't use TLS?

An Allow can't refuse requests, so it enforces nothing.
That condition concerns encryption headers, not TLS transport.
Denying 0.0.0.0/0 would block everything, not just plain HTTP.

versions.question: A bucket policy has a Deny whose condition is `aws:SecureTransport` = `false`. Which requests does it block?
options: Requests signed with Signature Version 2
Requests sent over plain HTTP
Requests that come from outside the VPC
Requests without a Content-MD5 header

option_explanations: The condition has nothing to do with signature version.
Correct. SecureTransport is false for plain HTTP requests.
The condition doesn't check network origin.
Content-MD5 isn't involved in this condition.

versions.question: Glacier Flexible Retrieval offers three retrieval speeds. Which one is meant for urgent needs, finishing within minutes?

versions.question: Application code written in Java needs to put objects into S3 as part of its normal logic. What is the right tool?

Globally replicated across every Region automatically

versions.question: A firm commits to a fixed hourly spend for one year and expects to stay in the M family and one Region but alter sizes and OS. Which purchase fits?

versions.question: Why does a web server's reply to an allowed inbound request on port 443 get out even though its security group has no matching outbound rule?
